Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

[{"id": "arka-english-main-1-prompt-long-0085", "row_sha256": "2059f3acb1a76923d1486283afffcc8ca8275c53b156c9e8794b0150e3c66421", "mode": "/prompt", "language": "en", "context": {}, "identity": false, "mode_instructions": "Organize the supplied request into a clear prompt. Preserve scope and constraints. Do not invent context, requirements, or missing information. Do not perform the task.", "input": "write an internal product update about the 4.8 browser extension change at trailmark, but make it read as one independent update, not a release note stitched to a support report. the preference is called “Open pinned pages in the background.” it belongs in Settings, under Tabs, and lets people choose whether pinned pages restored as part of startup or a manual session restore take focus immediately. right now the preference is off by default, so keep the existing behavior for people who do not turn it on: a restored pinned page can still become the active tab. don’t imply that this changes what happens for ordinary unpinned tabs.

i need the update to give enough background for people in product, support, and engineering to understand why we are changing this. some people keep work dashboards, calendars, and reference pages pinned for weeks, then restore a session and lose the place they were reading because a pinned page takes focus. we heard that in a small set of support conversations, but don’t present that as a measured survey or say how many users have the problem. the change is meant to give those users more control without changing the default for everyone else. it’s not a general tab management feature and it doesn’t change how a new pinned page opens when someone pins it during a session.

please explain the boundary of the behavior carefully. when someone turns the preference on, a pinned page restored during browser startup or through the manual restore-session command should open in the background. the page is still restored and remains pinned; it just does not take focus at that moment. a person can select it afterward as usual. this applies to those two restore paths only. it does not affect unpinned pages in a restored session, pinned pages opened directly from a bookmark, or a pinned page created while the browser is already running. don’t claim that it applies to mobile, because this preference is only in the desktop extension settings in this change.

for the implementation context, version 4.8 adds the preference on desktop for macos and windows. linux is not in this release and is being considered for 4.8.1, but that later version isn’t committed. signed-in users will have the setting synced between their desktop devices after the next settings sync. people who are signed out keep the value on that device only. if a user has no saved value when upgrading, leave the preference off; don’t migrate a different tab setting into it. the new toggle is visible in Settings under Tabs, after “Restore previous session.” mention this placement so support can point people to it.

we plan a staged rollout on the stable desktop channel, starting at 10% of eligible macos and windows users. if the first week shows no rise in restore-related crashes and the settings migration check passes, the team may raise exposure to 50% the following week. that increase is conditional, not a scheduled promise. don’t say the rollout has started or that either check has passed. telemetry for the toggle changing and for a restored pinned page taking focus is included in 4.8; it records the event and platform, not page titles or urls. users who have disabled optional diagnostics won’t send these events. make clear the telemetry describes behavior in aggregate and doesn’t identify what sites someone restored.

there’s one ordinary support quote we can use: “I open my laptop to get back to a report, and the pinned calendar keeps jumping in front of it.” include it once and make clear it came from a support conversation, not a formal research study. don’t embellish the quote or turn it into a claim about all users. the update should connect the quote to the narrow behavior change and then return to the specific release facts rather than turning the whole piece into a customer story.

please make the update around 650 to 800 words, with a useful title and connected paragraphs. use a short numbered section if it helps explain the two supported restore paths, but don’t force a list for every detail. include the preference name exactly, explain the default, platforms, sync distinction, rollout condition, and telemetry limits. keep the language plain and practical for the three internal audiences. the update should not be a promotional announcement and should not claim that the change fixes every focus problem or improves retention. distinguish what is in 4.8 from what is only being considered for 4.8.1.

finish with a separate assessment paragraph that states the current scope and the conditions for any move from 10% to 50%: the first-week crash check must show no rise in restore-related crashes, and the settings migration check must pass. describe the assessment as conditional; don’t report a result, recommend approval, or broaden the condition beyond this rollout decision. the final paragraph needs its own useful information about the limited desktop scope and the checks, not a recap of the whole update. don’t add a concluding summary after it.", "output": "Write an internal product update about Trailmark’s version 4.8 browser extension change. Make it a single, self-contained update for product, support, and engineering—not a release note joined to a support report. Use a practical, plain-language tone and a useful title. Aim for 650 to 800 words, with connected paragraphs. A short numbered section may clarify the supported restore paths, but do not force every detail into a list.

Explain the reason for the change: some people keep dashboards, calendars, and reference pages pinned for weeks, then lose their place when a restored pinned page takes focus. This came up in a small set of support conversations; do not describe it as a measured survey or quantify the number of affected users. The change gives those users more control while preserving the current default for everyone else. It is not a general tab-management feature.

The preference is named “Open pinned pages in the background.” It appears in desktop Settings under Tabs, after “Restore previous session.” When enabled, it keeps a pinned page restored through either of these paths from taking focus immediately:
1. Browser startup.
2. The manual restore-session command.

The page is still restored and remains pinned, and users can select it afterward as usual. The preference does not change what happens to unpinned pages in a restored session, pinned pages opened directly from a bookmark, or pages pinned during an active session. It does not apply to mobile. The preference is off by default, so users who do not enable it retain the existing behavior: a restored pinned page may become the active tab. Do not imply that this changes the behavior of ordinary unpinned tabs or newly pinned pages.

For version 4.8, the preference is available on desktop for macOS and Windows. Linux is not included in this release and is being considered for 4.8.1; do not present that later version as committed. For signed-in users, the setting syncs between desktop devices after the next settings sync. For signed-out users, it is stored only on the device. When upgrading, a user with no saved value keeps the preference off. Do not migrate any other tab setting into it.

Describe the planned rollout on the stable desktop channel: it starts at 10% of eligible macOS and Windows users. The team may raise exposure to 50% the following week only if the first week shows no rise in restore-related crashes and the settings migration check passes. This increase is conditional, not a scheduled promise. Do not state that the rollout has begun or that either check has passed.

Version 4.8 includes telemetry for changes to the toggle and for a restored pinned page taking focus. It records the event and platform, not page titles or URLs. Users who have disabled optional diagnostics will not send these events. Explain that the telemetry describes behavior in aggregate and does not identify which sites someone restored.

Include this support-conversation quote exactly once: “I open my laptop to get back to a report, and the pinned calendar keeps jumping in front of it.” Identify it as coming from a support conversation, not a formal research study. Do not embellish it or present it as representative of all users. Connect it to the narrow behavior change, then return to the specific release facts.

Do not make the update promotional or claim that the change fixes every focus problem or improves retention. Distinguish clearly between what is included in 4.8 and what is only being considered for 4.8.1.

End with a separate assessment paragraph that states the current desktop scope and the conditions for a possible move from 10% to 50%: the first-week check must show no rise in restore-related crashes, and the settings migration check must pass. Keep this assessment conditional. Do not report a result, recommend approval, or broaden the conditions beyond this rollout decision. Give the final paragraph useful information about the limited desktop scope and those checks; do not add a summary after it."}]
